hints: Notice the series connection, so the filament lamp also carries the same $0.34\text{ A}$ current as the fixed resistor.
On the filament lamp $I$-$V$ graph, find $0.34\text{ A}$ on the $I$-axis and read horizontally then down to the $V$-axis to get the lamp voltage.
Use $R = V/I$ for the lamp at that operating point, with $V$ about $4\text{ V}$ and $I = 0.34\text{ A}$, and check the unit is $\Omega$.
walkthrough: In series the current is the same everywhere, so $I_{lamp} = I_{resistor} = 0.34\text{ A}$.
The lamp is non-ohmic, so its resistance must be found from its actual $V$ and $I$ using $R = V/I$, not from a gradient.
Read the filament lamp graph at $I = 0.34\text{ A}$: go across from $0.34$ on the $I/\text{A}$ axis to the curve, then down to the $V/\text{V}$ axis.
Calculate $R_{lamp} \approx 11.8\text{ }\Omega$, about $12\text{ }\Omega$ with sensible precision. This is option B.

A.explanation: This is about $0.081$ S, the value of $I/V$ at $0.34\text{ A}$, which is conductance not resistance $R = V/I$.

B.explanation: At $0.34\text{ A}$ the lamp graph gives $V \approx 4.0\text{ V}$, so $R = V/I \approx 4.0/0.34 \approx 12\text{ }\Omega$.

C.explanation: This results from reading too large a lamp voltage of about $5\text{ V}$ at $0.34\text{ A}$ instead of about $4.0\text{ V}$.

D.explanation: This is the resistance of the fixed resistor, where $0.34\text{ A}$ corresponds to about $6.0\text{ V}$, not the lamp.
